questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply agent designs to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the synthetic feature engineering below, a learner yields these values. Consider agent designs: an agent selects each action using only the percept it receives at this instant. It keeps no record of earlier observations and builds no model of how the environment evolves. Which agent design does this description match? Reason from the given facts, precisely.

options.text: A simple reflex agent acting only on the current percept.
A model-based reflex agent tracking hidden state.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the agent maintains any state at all.

options.text: A goal-based agent planning toward a target state.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes explicit goals and lookahead search.

options.text: A utility-based agent maximizing expected satisfaction.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes a utility function over outcomes.

questions.explanation: A simple reflex agent maps the current percept directly to an action through condition-action rules, with no memory or world model. The description explicitly denies stored history and an environment model, ruling out model-based, goal-based, and utility-based designs, each of which needs internal state beyond the present percept.
questions.hint: Ask whether the agent stores anything beyond the percept in front of it.

questions.learningObjective: Apply heuristics to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Taking 0, 12 and 7 as the given figures, on a four-connected grid an agent starts at (0, 0) and must reach a goal at (12, 7). Each unit step costs 1 and no obstacles are present. What is the Manhattan-distance heuristic value at the starting state? Give the exact answer, using only the information above.

options.misconception: Undercounts by assuming the goal square needs no move
Uses the area of the rectangle instead of step distance
Counts only the larger coordinate displacement

questions.explanation: Manhattan distance adds the absolute coordinate differences: |12 - 0| + |7 - 0| = 12 + 7 = 19. Because there are no diagonal moves, this is also the exact optimal path cost. Multiplying coordinates, dropping one step, or keeping only the larger displacement each fails to sum both coordinate gaps and so understates the distance.
questions.hint: Sum the horizontal and vertical separations independently.

questions.learningObjective: Apply adversarial search to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Taking 9, 5 and 6 as the given figures, a two-ply game tree has a MAX root with two MIN children. The first MIN child has leaves 9 and 5; the second MIN child has leaves 6 and 8. Under minimax with both players choosing optimally, what value is backed up to the root?

options.misconception: Swaps the roles of MAX and MIN at the two levels
Assumes MAX gets to pick a leaf directly
Assumes MIN chooses at the root

questions.explanation: Minimax backs up values from the leaves. Each MIN child takes the smaller of its leaves, giving 5 and 6. The MAX root then takes the larger of those, 6. Taking maxima at the MIN level swaps the players, while taking a global maximum or minimum ignores the alternating levels entirely, so each of those answers misapplies the recurrence.
questions.hint: Evaluate the bottom MIN nodes first, then let the root MAX choose between them.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply informed search to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the informed search scenario (case 3304), a heuristic h satisfies h(n) <= h*(n) for every state n, where h*(n) is the true optimal cost from n to a goal. Which property does h necessarily have? Reason from the given facts, precisely.

options.text: Admissible: it never overestimates the true cost to the goal.
Consistent: it obeys the triangle inequality on every arc.
options.misconception: Wrongly names the stronger arcwise condition.

options.text: Monotone: its value never decreases along a path.
options.misconception: Wrongly states the opposite of the usual monotonicity direction.

options.text: Optimal: it guarantees the best path without any search.
options.misconception: Wrongly claims a bound alone searches the space.

questions.explanation: The inequality h(n) <= h*(n) is exactly the definition of admissibility: the estimate never overestimates the remaining cost. Consistency is a stronger condition involving arc costs between neighboring states, and a heuristic being admissible does not by itself make search instantaneous or optimal without the surrounding algorithm guarantees. The competing options name different or invented properties.
questions.hint: Compare the estimate to the true remaining cost, not to neighbor costs.

questions.learningObjective: Apply bayesian inference to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Suppose the values are 0.18, 0.83, and 0.86; a disease has prevalence 0.18. A test detects it with sensitivity 0.83 when present and has specificity 0.86 when absent. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability, to four decimals, that this person actually has the disease?

options.misconception: Reports sensitivity and ignores the base rate
Reports the prior probability of disease
Reports only the joint numerator, unnormalized

questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem gives P(D|+) = se*p / (se*p + (1 - sp)*(1 - p)) = 0.149 / (0.149 + 0.115) = 0.5655. The numerator alone is not a probability because it is unnormalized, and the sensitivity or the prior each ignore the false-positive contributions and the base rate, which is precisely the base-rate fallacy.
questions.hint: Compute true positives and false positives over a population, then take the true-positive share.

questions.stem: Suppose the values are 0.7, 0.5, and 0.4; in a Bayesian network with edge A -> B, the prior is P(A) = 0.7. The conditional table gives P(B | A) = 0.5 and P(B | not A) = 0.4. What is the joint probability P(A and B), to four decimals? Give the exact answer.

options.misconception: Uses the conditional probability of the wrong parent state
Computes the marginal probability of the child instead
Reports the conditional probability and ignores the parent

questions.explanation: The joint distribution factorizes as P(A, B) = P(A) * P(B | A) = 0.7 * 0.5 = 0.35. Adding the contribution from not A computes the marginal P(B), and using P(B | not A) or the conditional alone does not follow the factorization for the event A and B together.
questions.hint: Multiply the parent's prior by the child's conditional given that parent state.

questions.stem: Considering propositional logic, case 3307 — given the truth assignment P = true, Q = false, R = true, evaluate the propositional formula (P and Q) or (not P and R). Which statement is correct? Report the result.

options.text: False, because neither disjunct holds.
True, because at least one disjunct holds.
options.misconception: Reverses the truth value of the disjunction.

options.text: True, but only when R is false.
options.misconception: Wrongly ties the value to R rather than to the disjuncts.

options.text: Undetermined without knowing Q and R together.
options.misconception: Wrongly claims the truth value cannot be evaluated.

questions.explanation: With P = true and Q = false, the first conjunct P and Q is false. With not P = false and R = true, the second conjunct is false. The disjunction of false and false is false, so neither disjunct holds. The alternatives either invert the result or wrongly claim the value is undecidable when all atoms are assigned.
questions.hint: Evaluate each conjunction first, then combine them with or.

options.misconception: Performs gradient ascent by flipping the update sign
Drops the factor of two from the derivative
Ignores the learning rate entirely

questions.explanation: The gradient at w = 8 is 2(8 - 4) = 8. The descent update is w - lr * grad = 8 - 0.2 * (8) = 6.4. Adding the gradient instead ascends the loss, dropping the factor of two uses the wrong derivative, and omitting the learning rate takes a full-size step, so each alternative is a distinct calculus or step-size error.

questions.stem: A regressor predicts 9, 5, 6 for three examples whose true targets are 8, 5, 9. What is the mean squared error of these predictions, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Uses mean absolute error instead of squared error
Forgets to divide by the number of examples
Corrupts the first residual by adding instead of subtracting

questions.explanation: The squared residuals are (9 - 8)^2, (5 - 5)^2, and (6 - 9)^2, summing to 10. Dividing by the three examples gives 3.3333. Mean absolute error squares nothing, skipping the division reports the total rather than the mean, and adding in any residual uses the wrong sign, so those values are not the MSE.
questions.hint: Square each prediction-minus-target residual, add them, then divide by three.

questions.stem: With the data 39 / 6 / 8 in view, a classifier's confusion matrix reports 39 true positives, 6 false positives, and 8 false negatives. What is the F1 score for the positive class, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Reports precision and ignores recall
Reports recall and ignores precision
Uses a simplified accuracy that drops true negatives

questions.hint: Compute precision and recall, then take their harmonic mean.

Subtracts the intercept instead of adding it
Multiplies the features instead of weighting them

questions.stem: In the synthetic feature engineering below, a learner gives the following estimate. A logistic regression model computes a logit of z = -2.5 for a given input. What is the predicted probability of the positive class, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, precisely.

options.misconception: Flips the exponent sign, inverting the sigmoid
Uses a linear-ratio substitute for the sigmoid
Reports the complement probability of the positive class

questions.explanation: The sigmoid maps a logit z to 1/(1 + e^{-z}) = 1/(1 + e^{--2.5}) = 0.0759. Reversing the exponent sign gives the complement, the linear-ratio substitute is not the logistic function, and reporting 1 minus the probability gives the negative-class probability. Only the sigmoid transformation is correct.

Class 0

options.text: Class 2
options.misconception: Invents a class not present among the nearest neighbors

options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the votes are evenly split

questions.stem: The case uses 0.8, 0.5 and 0.6; a naive Bayes classifier has class prior 0.8. Given two observed features, the class-conditional likelihoods for the positive class are 0.5 and 0.6, and for the negative class they are 0.5 and 0.3. What is the posterior probability of the positive class, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Reports the unnormalized numerator as if it were a posterior
Uses a single likelihood and ignores the other evidence
Reports the prior and ignores the observed features

questions.explanation: Naive Bayes multiplies likelihoods under the conditional-independence assumption: the positive score is 0.8*0.5*0.6 = 0.24 and the negative score is (1-0.8)*0.5*0.3 = 0.03. questions.stem: The case uses 12, 7; a decision-tree leaf contains 12 examples of one class and 7 of the other. What is the Gini impurity of this leaf, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, using only the information above.

Uses only the majority fraction, not squared shares
Computes entropy instead of Gini impurity

Reports the weight norm instead of the margin width
Uses the sum of components instead of the Euclidean norm

Uses the maximum instead of the centroid mean
Averages only two of the three points

Inverts the numerator and denominator
Adds a spurious five to the support of A

questions.stem: Working from 6, 8, and 0, a linear support vector machine has weight vector w = (6, 8). What is the width of the margin between the two separating hyperplanes w·x + b0 = 1 and w·x + b0 = -1, to four decimals? Report the result, and state the conclusion.

options.misconception: Reports the weight norm instead of the margin width
Reports half the margin, forgetting the factor of two
Uses the sum of components instead of the Euclidean norm

questions.explanation: The two hyperplanes are separated by 2/||w||. Here ||w|| = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = 10, so the width is 2/10 = 0.2. Reporting 1/||w|| gives only half the gap, the norm itself is not a distance between planes, and dividing by the component sum uses the wrong norm.
questions.hint: Compute the Euclidean norm of the weight vector, then divide two by it.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply clustering to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Set 7 alongside 13 before reading on: in a k-means update step, one cluster contains the three one-dimensional points 7, 7, and 13. What is the new centroid (cluster mean) for these points, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Uses the maximum instead of the centroid mean
Uses the median rather than the k-means mean
Averages only two of the three points

questions.explanation: The k-means centroid is the arithmetic mean of assigned points: (7 + 7 + 13) / 3 = 9. The median, the maximum, and an average that drops one point are each different statistics that do not minimize the cluster's squared error the way the mean does.
questions.hint: Add all three coordinates and divide by the number of points.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply dimensionality reduction to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: A PCA fit reports eigenvalues 30, 11, and 4 for the first three principal components. What fraction of the total variance is explained by the first principal component alone, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Reports the variance of the first two components combined
Divides by one eigenvalue instead of the total variance
Reports the raw eigenvalue, not a fraction of variance

questions.explanation: The proportion of variance explained by a component is its eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues. The total is 30 + 11 + 4 = 45, so the first component explains 30/45 = 0.6667. Using one eigenvalue as the denominator, combining two components, or reporting the raw eigenvalue does not give the fraction for the first component alone.
questions.hint: Divide the leading eigenvalue by the sum of all reported eigenvalues.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply association rules to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Set 22 alongside 13 before reading on: in a transaction dataset, itemset A appears in 22 transactions and the combined itemset A and B appears in 13 transactions. What is the confidence of the association rule A -> B, to four decimals? Give the exact answer.

options.misconception: Inverts the numerator and denominator
Divides by a made-up transaction total rather than support of A
Adds a spurious five to the support of A

questions.explanation: Confidence of A -> B is support(A and B) / support(A) = 13/22 = 0.5909. It measures how often B occurs among transactions containing A. Dividing by an invented total, inverting the ratio, or padding the denominator all fail to compute the conditional frequency that confidence represents.
questions.hint: Confidence is the support of the union divided by the support of the antecedent.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply perceptrons to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: A bipolar perceptron has weights w1 = -1, w2 = -1 and bias 1. For inputs x1 = 0, x2 = -2, it outputs +1 when the weighted sum is nonnegative and -1 otherwise. What is its output?

options.misconception: Uses a binary zero/one step instead of the bipolar step
Flips the sign of the step function output
Reports the weighted sum, not the thresholded output

questions.explanation: The weighted sum is -1(0) + -1(-2) + 1 = 3. Since 3 is nonnegative, the bipolar step outputs 1. Flipping the sign misstates the step, zero belongs to a binary step, and the raw sum skips thresholding entirely.
questions.hint: Compute the weighted sum, then apply the bipolar threshold at zero.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply activation functions to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the synthetic feature engineering below, a classifier computes this result. An activation function receives input x = 1.5. For the sigmoid, what is the activation value at this input, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, with the definitions in mind.

options.misconception: Uses a linear-ratio substitute
Reverses the exponent sign
Uses tanh, whose range is negative one to one

questions.explanation: Evaluating the sigmoid at 1.5 gives 0.8176. Each alternative corresponds to a different function or a sign/clipping mistake: swapping a sigmoid for tanh changes the range, reversing an exponent sign inverts a sigmoid, and forgetting rectification lets negative values pass through a ReLU. Only the correct function and argument yield 0.8176.
questions.hint: Recall the definition and output range of the sigmoid, then substitute x.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply network architecture to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: A fully connected (dense) neural layer receives 8 inputs and has 6 output units, with one bias term per output unit. How many trainable parameters does the layer have?

options.misconception: Adds rather than multiplies inputs and units
Omits the bias connections to each unit
Adds a spurious bias row and column

questions.explanation: Each of the 6 output units has 8 incoming weights plus one bias, so the layer has (8 + 1) * 6 = 54 trainable parameters. Omitting biases drops one per unit, adding rather than multiplying miscounts the weight matrix, and adding a bias column overcounts by an entire row of weights.
questions.hint: Count weights plus one bias for each output unit.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply convolutional networks to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: On the figures 30, 3, 1, a convolution operates on an input of spatial size 30 with a filter of size 3, padding P = 1 on each side, and stride S = 1. Using the standard integer floor formula, what is the output spatial size?

options.misconception: Assumes unit stride and no padding
Ignores the zero-padding term
Off-by-one: forgets the leading output position

questions.explanation: The output size is floor((W - F + 2P)/S) + 1 = floor((30 - 3 + 2)/1) + 1 = 30. Dropping padding, assuming stride one with no padding, or omitting the final plus one each changes the counted positions and gives a wrong dimension.
questions.hint: Apply floor((W - F + 2P)/S) and remember the leading one.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply value functions to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Suppose the values are 4, 8, and 6; in a Q-learning update, taking action a in state s yields an immediate reward of 4 and leads to state s'. From s' the best action has Q-value 8 (the two successor Q-values are 8 and 6), and the discount factor is gamma = 0.9. What is the target value r + gamma * max Q(s', a'), to four decimals?

options.misconception: Forgets to discount the future value
Uses the first successor value instead of the maximum
Sums successor values instead of taking the maximum

questions.explanation: The one-step target is r + gamma * max_a' Q(s', a') = 4 + 0.9 * 8 = 11.2. Using one successor value ignores the maximization, dropping the discount fails to reduce future rewards, and summing successors double-counts the future. The Bellman optimality target requires exactly the maximum of the successor values.
questions.hint: Take the largest successor Q-value, discount it, and add the immediate reward.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply returns and discounting to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Suppose the values are 3, 5, and 0.8; an agent receives rewards 3, 3, 5 at three successive time steps with discount factor gamma = 0.8. What is the discounted return G0 = r0 + gamma*r1 + gamma^2*r2, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Drops the third reward entirely
Sums rewards with no discounting
Discounts the immediate reward as well

questions.explanation: The discounted return weights each reward by gamma raised to its time index: 3 + 0.8*3 + 0.8^2*5 = 8.6. Summing without discount treats future rewards as equal to immediate ones, dropping the last term truncates the horizon, and applying gamma to the first reward discounts the immediate reward, which the definition does not do.
questions.hint: Raise gamma to the power of each reward's time index before summing.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply term weighting to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Working from 3, 47, and 8, a term appears 3 times in a document. In a corpus of 47 documents it appears in 8 documents. Using tf-idf with natural-log inverse document frequency idf = ln(N/df), what is the term's tf-idf weight in this document, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Reports inverse document frequency alone, ignoring term frequency
Uses a base-ten logarithm instead of the natural logarithm
Omits the logarithm in the idf factor

questions.explanation: The inverse document frequency is ln(47/8) = 1.7707. Multiplying by the term frequency gives 3 * 1.7707 = 5.3121. A base-ten logarithm changes the scale, idf alone ignores how often the term appears here, and dropping the logarithm produces a ratio far larger than the log-scaled weight.
questions.hint: Compute ln(N/df) first, then multiply by the term frequency.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply attention to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the synthetic feature engineering below, a agent produces the following output. Working from 1, 2, a softmax attention head computes unnormalized scores s1 = -1 and s2 = -1 for two keys. What attention weight is assigned to the first key, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, showing the key step.

options.misconception: Reports the unnormalized exponential
Normalizes raw scores instead of exponentiating them
Reports the weight of the wrong score

questions.explanation: Softmax exponentiates each score and normalizes: e^-1 / (e^-1 + e^-1) = 0.3679 / (0.3679 + 0.3679) = 0.5. Normalizing the raw scores ignores the exponential, reporting e^-1 alone is unnormalized, and the complementary weight belongs to the second key. Only the softmax of the first score is correct.
questions.hint: Exponentiate both scores, divide the first exponential by their sum.

questions.learningObjective: Apply language model evaluation to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Working from 2.5, 2, a language model has a cross-entropy of 2.5 bits per token on a held-out corpus. What is its perplexity (base 2), to three decimals? Give the exact answer, step by step.

options.misconception: Doubles the entropy rather than exponentiating
Squares the entropy instead of exponentiating it
Raises two to H+1 instead of to H

questions.explanation: Perplexity is defined as 2 raised to the cross-entropy in bits per token: 2^2.5 = 5.657. Squaring or doubling the entropy are not the definition, and using base ten would correspond to entropy measured in nats or decimal digits rather than bits.
questions.hint: Perplexity is two to the power of the per-token cross-entropy in bits.

questions.learningObjective: Apply fairness metrics to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the synthetic feature engineering below, a agent returns the reported scores. A binary classifier selects group A at rate 0.4 and group B at rate 0.4. What is the demographic-parity difference between the two groups, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, using only the information above.

options.misconception: Multiplies the two rates rather than differencing them
Reports the ratio of rates instead of their difference
Adds the rates instead of taking their difference

questions.explanation: Demographic parity difference is the absolute gap in positive selection rates: |0.4 - 0.4| = 0. A ratio, a product, or a sum of the two rates measures something different from the difference the demographic-parity criterion uses, so each of those is a distinct misreading of the metric.
questions.hint: Take the absolute value of one selection rate minus the other.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply data leakage to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the synthetic feature engineering below, a agent yields these values. Examine data leakage: a practitioner computes feature means and scaling parameters over the entire labeled dataset, and only afterward splits the data into training and test sets, then reports an unusually high test accuracy. What is the most likely flaw in this procedure? Reason from the given facts, carefully.

options.text: Class imbalance: one label dominates the dataset.
options.misconception: Wrongly diagnoses label skew, which is not described.

options.text: Underfitting: the model is too simple for the task.
options.misconception: Wrongly blames model capacity instead of information flow.

options.text: Overfitting from too few training epochs.
options.misconception: Wrongly attributes the issue to training duration.

options.text: Leakage: test-set statistics influenced the training pipeline.

questions.explanation: Because the scaling statistics were computed before the split, information from the test set leaked into the transformation applied during training. This data leakage inflates test performance because the held-out examples influenced preprocessing. The other options name unrelated problems: model capacity, label distribution, and training duration are not implicated by preprocessing on the full dataset.
questions.hint: Ask whether any test-set information entered the pipeline before the split.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply decision thresholds to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the synthetic feature engineering below, a agent gives the following estimate. Examine decision thresholds: a probabilistic classifier outputs a score for the positive class. If the decision threshold for predicting positive is raised while the model and data stay fixed, what generally happens to recall and precision? Reason from the given facts, carefully.

options.text: Recall rises while precision tends to fall.
options.misconception: Describes the effect of lowering, not raising, the threshold.

options.text: Both precision and recall rise together.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the two metrics move in the same direction.

options.text: Neither metric changes with the threshold.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes threshold and metrics are independent.

options.text: Recall falls while precision tends to rise.

questions.explanation: Raising the threshold makes positive predictions harder to earn, so fewer true positives are captured and recall falls. The predictions that remain positive are on average more confident, so precision tends to rise. Lowering the threshold produces the opposite pattern, and the two metrics do trade off, so they cannot both move together or stay fixed in general.
questions.hint: Consider which predictions are relabeled when the cutoff moves upward.
